The Striped piggy, Pomadasys stridens, attains an ultimate total length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters], a modest size for a coastal haemulid. This maximum length corresponds to an ultimate wet weight estimated at 110 grams [Wwi = 110 grams]. In contrast, the onset of reproductive maturity is marked by a far smaller body size; individuals typically reach puberty at a total length of roughly 11 centimeters [Lp = roughly 11 centimeters]. At this developmental milestone, the associated wet weight is approximately 18.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 18.4 grams], reflecting the considerable somatic growth that must occur between the initiation of gonadal activity and the achievement of full adult dimensions. Field surveys in the northwestern Indian Ocean suggest these size thresholds are relatively consistent across the species’ range, though local environmental conditions may introduce some variation.

Focusing on early life stages, the hatchlings of Pomadasys stridens emerge from pelagic eggs at a remarkably diminutive size. This minimal initial mass is typical of species with a pelagic larval phase that must transition quickly to exogenous feeding. This high fecundity, typical of many serially spawning teleosts, compensates for the low survival probability of planktonic eggs and larvae.

Lifespan and the timing of reproduction are further constrained by temperature. For Pomadasys stridens, the maximum recorded longevity in the wild is estimated at approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] when considering the thermal regime of its typical habitat, which is at 25.2 °C [T = 25.2 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan for a fish of its body size is characteristic of a slow-paced life history strategy, allowing multiple reproductive seasons. The age at first spawning, which typically follows shortly after the attainment of sexual maturity, is estimated to occur within a few months of puberty, although precise field data for the Striped piggy remain scarce. Comparisons with other haemulids suggest that the trade-off between early reproduction and continued somatic growth is finely balanced in this species.

The overall life history profile of Pomadasys stridens aligns with that of a moderate-sized, iteroparous teleost inhabiting warm, productive coastal ecosystems.
